To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the President of the Republic, in Argentina, is not a mere representative of the will of the people but rather a powerful political figure who is able to influence the political process and to make policy.
the Argentine presidential power is limited by the institutional framework and by political conditions.

the policy of privatisation in Argentina during the nineties, which was a radical change in the state's role in the economy, was approved thanks to the institutional capacity of the presidency to enact reforms and the strong partisan support the president enjoyed in Congress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the institutional relations between President and Congress in Argentina, and how these relations affect the capacity of the President to enact policy reforms.
how presidents are able to use their powers to achieve policy objectives.

the institutional relations that the Presidency has with Congress, but also with the way in which the political context influences those relations and, therefore, the institutional power of the Presidency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Argentine regime is characterised by a mixture of presidential centralism and limited presidentialism.
, in Argentina, presidents are not hyper-powerful but they are not powerless either.
, in the case of Argentina, the Presidency has been able to enact policy reforms only when the President has had a solid base of partisan support in Congress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the institutional relations between the President and Congress are not fixed, but rather depend upon the political context.
the article shows that presidential power is not an unchanging and unchallengeable feature of the Argentine political system, but rather a variable and dynamic one.
we have found that the Argentine presidential system is not as centralised as it is usually described.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the President is a central figure in the Argentine political arena, the President's institutional power is not absolute.
the institutional capacity of presidents to enact policy reform is not only a function of the constitutional resources they enjoy, but also a function of their political resources.
the institutional relations between Congress and the Executive are a crucial factor for understanding the dynamics of presidential power in Argentina and the policy-making process in general.
